issues.legal_issue: A rule deeming an undecided mining-lease renewal application refused for the purpose of revision, and fixing the date for seeking revision, is within the rule-making power and is not unreasonable or contrary to the governing statute.
material_facts: A lease to mine a scheduled mineral on government land had been granted to the applicants’ father before the governing Act came into force.
After his death, the applicants sought renewal, but the State Government did not dispose of the application within the prescribed period.
The applicants challenged the deemed refusal and the rule governing revision, arguing that the rules were unreasonable and inconsistent with the statutory provisions for renewal.
The governing scheme made renewal subject to the Act and rules, and required central approval for granting renewal of a lease for the mineral, but not for refusing renewal.
The rules provided a route for revision to the Central Government, which could make an order it considered just and proper.
issues.conclusion: The amended renewal-disposal rule did not itself deem a renewal application refused, but the explanation to the revision rule treated the State Government’s failure to decide within the prescribed period as a refusal for revision purposes and set the date from which the revision period ran. Those provisions were within the rule-making power and were neither unreasonable nor contrary to the Act.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 4, 8, 13(2)(g), 19, 20 and 30 of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) Act, 1957, read with Rules 24 and 54 of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960, establish a regulatory scheme governing grants and renewals. Section 13(2)(g) permits rules on the terms and conditions for granting or renewing leases, including conditions for refusal. Rights in government mineral land arise under the Act and rules, not independently of them. The deeming provision enables an applicant to seek revision when the State does not decide within the prescribed time; the requirement of central approval applies to granting renewal, not refusing it. The Court distinguished Shivji Nathubhai v. Union of India, [1960] 2 SCR 775, and the decision in C.A. No. 657 of 1967 as addressing the Central Government’s quasi-judicial revisional power, not the State Government’s power to grant or refuse a lease; it also referred to Seeta Ramaiah v. State of Andhra Pradesh, AIR 1963 AP 54, and Shivji Nathubhai v. Union of India, AIR 1959 Punjab 510.

rule.if: challenge_to_deemed_refusal_rule and government_controlled_mineral_lease and renewal_application_not_decided_within_deadline and lease_rights_derive_from_regulatory_scheme and revision_route_available

predicates.challenge_to_deemed_refusal_rule: A party in a proceeding challenging a rule applies for renewal of a mining lease and contests the legal effect of the government’s failure to decide it on time.
predicates.government_controlled_mineral_lease: The lease concerns mineral land controlled by the government.
predicates.renewal_application_not_decided_within_d: The government does not decide a renewal application within the prescribed period.
predicates.lease_rights_derive_from_regulatory_sche: The rights to obtain or renew the lease arise under the governing regulatory scheme rather than independently of it.
predicates.revision_route_available: The regulatory scheme permits an aggrieved applicant to seek review of a refusal or deemed refusal by a higher government authority.

issues.definition: When a party challenges the deemed refusal of a renewal application for a government-controlled mineral lease that was not decided on time, and the lease rights and review route arise from the regulatory scheme, the deeming and revision rules are valid.

issues.legal_issue: Rejecting a revision application as time-barred is not unreasonable where it was filed outside the permitted period and the record before the revising authority contained the relevant facts.
material_facts: The applicants sought revision after the State Government informed them that their renewal application was deemed refused.
They filed the revision application more than two months after that communication and could also have sought revision after the decision period had elapsed without a response.
The Central Government rejected the revision application as time-barred after stating that it had carefully considered the facts in the application.
The revision application contained the relevant facts, and the applicants did not establish a basis for extending the filing period.
issues.conclusion: There was no reason to regard the Central Government’s rejection of the revision application as unreasonable; the Court set aside the High Court’s contrary order.
issues.legal_principle: Rule 54(1) of the Mineral Concession Rules, 1960, requires an application for revision to be filed within two months, but permits a late application where sufficient cause is shown. The explanation to Rule 54 identifies when a failure to decide an application is treated as a refusal for purposes of revision. Shivji Nathubhai v. Union of India, [1960] 2 SCR 775, and the decision in C.A. No. 657 of 1967 establish that the Central Government’s power under Rule 54 is quasi-judicial. The Court found no basis to assume the authority had failed to consider the facts presented to it.

rule.if: challenge_to_revision_rejection and revision_filed_after_review_period and relevant_facts_presented_to_revising_authority and no_sufficient_cause_established

predicates.challenge_to_revision_rejection: A party in a proceeding challenges the higher authority’s rejection of an application seeking review of a government decision.
predicates.revision_filed_after_review_period: The applicant files the review application after the period allowed for doing so has elapsed.
predicates.relevant_facts_presented_to_revising_aut: The review application placed the relevant case facts before the revising authority.
predicates.no_sufficient_cause_established: The applicant does not establish a sufficient reason for filing the review application late.

issues.definition: When a party challenges a review rejection, filed late with the relevant facts before the authority and without established sufficient cause, the time-barred rejection is not unreasonable.
